bib.title: MAG-V: A Multi-Agent Framework for Synthetic Data Generation and Verification

question: How can an enterprise generate realistic test queries for a tool-calling agent and verify the agent's tool-call trajectory without an LLM judge?
hypothesis: If questions similar to a base question follow the same trajectory, confidence in the assistant's reasoning pathway is higher; high trajectory variance means lower confidence.
contributions: Using agents to create synthetic data aligned with specific requirements.
A deterministic method for verifying agent trajectories that does not rely on LLMs for feedback.
Simple ML baselines with feature engineering can match more expensive and capable models.

method.summary: Investigator agent writes synthetic customer-style questions from 19 seed questions via ICL; the assistant answers each 5 times and the most common trajectory is annotated by experts. For verification, a reverse-engineer agent writes 3 alternate questions from the response, the assistant answers them, similarity features between base and alternate trajectories feed classical ML classifiers, compared with GPT-4 and GPT-4o judges.
method.task: binary classification of agent tool-call trajectory correctness; synthetic query generation

datasets.name: Seed questions
datasets.source: written by one internal engineer to meet product requirements

datasets.name: Synthetic MAG-V questions
datasets.size: 190 generated, 55 after clustering, 45 after manual removal; 30 incorrect and 15 correct trajectories
datasets.split: stratified 10-fold CV (5-fold for the feature ablation); 3 seeds
datasets.source: generated by GPT-4o-mini investigator; Splunk observability-style tool environment (platform details unreleased)
datasets.preprocessing: BGE embeddings (R1024), UMAP to R2, HDBSCAN gives 11 clusters, top-5 nearest centroid per cluster = 55, remove 10 generic or in-development = 45

other.use: investigator, reverse engineer, assistant during data generation
assistant during verification; also judge baseline

models.name: Random Forest, Logistic Regression, Naive Bayes, k-NN, SVM, Decision Tree, XGBoost

other.k-NN: k=5 without arguments, k=4 with arguments; others default settings

other.features: EM, EDIT, GEDIT, SS (BGE-Large cosine), AO, LCSS between base and each alternate trajectory, plus TF-IDF of base question; with/without tool arguments

inference.samples: each of 45 questions run 5 times by assistant, most common trajectory kept; 3 alternate questions per base question
inference.prompting: ICL: each sample has trajectory T1, question Q1, and trajectory T2 sampled from seed; investigator executes T2 and writes 10 questions in the style of Q1. Judge baselines: annotation rubric, label order switched, rationale before score, one correct and one incorrect Q+T example, with and without Autogen default system prompt 'You are a helpful AI Assistant.'

metrics.name: Accuracy
metrics.definition: mean over folds and 3 seeds of agreement with expert label

metrics.name: F1
metrics.definition: mean over folds and 3 seeds; positive class not stated

baselines: GPT-4o judge, with and without system prompt
eval.protocol: Judges tested on same test splits and seeds as CV. Labels: two domain experts, third expert breaks ties.

availability.data: platform details to be released upon publication

results.claim: k-NN with all features and arguments matches the GPT-4 judge in accuracy (82.33 vs 82.83).
results.setup: 45 annotated trajectories, 10-fold stratified CV, 3 seeds, all features, GPT-4 with system prompt
results.quote: While our k-NN model (82.33%) matches GPT-4 in accuracy (82.83%), it lags behind in F1 (71.73 vs. 76.06)
results.note: Read from Fig 2 and text; Table 1 (5-fold, EDIT only) gives GPT-4 82.22 and GPT-4o 71.11, different setup

results.claim: k-NN improves over the GPT-4o judge by about 11% accuracy and 4% F1.
results.setup: as above; GPT-4o with system prompt
results.quote: our k-NN model shows 11% accuracy and 4% F1 improvement over GPT-4o
results.note: Abstract says outperforms GPT-4o judge by 11% accuracy; unclear if absolute points or relative

results.claim: Adding the default system prompt raises GPT-4o judge accuracy by about 12%, showing prompt sensitivity.
results.setup: GPT-4o judge, same 45 trajectories, with vs without 'You are a helpful AI Assistant.'
results.quote: the accuracy of GPT-4o increases by about 12%

results.claim: Using only EDIT distance, Random Forest and XGBoost reach 80% accuracy vs GPT-4o 71.11 and GPT-4 82.22.
results.setup: six trajectory features with arguments, 5-fold CV, 3 seeds; best feature subset was EDIT alone
results.table: Table 1, rows Random Forest and XGBoost, column Accuracy (F1 75.3)
results.note: GPT-4 row 82.22 accuracy, F1 77.94; GPT-4o F1 69.85

results.claim: Every ML model benefits from including tool arguments in the features.
results.setup: Fig 2, all 7 ML models, with vs without arguments

results.claim: Annotator agreement on trajectory correctness was moderate.
results.setup: two domain experts, agreed on 34 of 45

results.claim: Anecdote: adding the 45 synthetic questions and trajectories as ICL examples let a GPT-4o-mini assistant find the correct time range on one real customer query where it otherwise failed after 10 retries.
results.setup: single real query, GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini assistant

limits: Only 45 annotated trajectories (30 incorrect, 15 correct), one proprietary domain; authors say they need to test how the method scales with samples.
Moderate annotator agreement (kappa 0.42); authors note some incorrect trajectories could be marked correct.
k-NN lags GPT-4 in F1 (71.73 vs 76.06).
Method needs 3 extra questions and trajectories per item, so more API calls.
Only trajectory verified, not the response answer.
Synthetic-data benefit shown on one anecdotal query; no quantitative result despite the abstract's claim.
Platform and data unreleased; no code link; GPT judge runs use default parameters, so judge non-determinism is not quantified.
Standard errors across seeds not reported; accuracy comparisons on 45 items are noisy.
